rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, two-year (2012-2013) field experiment at Bushland TX with a wireless IRT sensor network controlling a VRI center pivot, RCBD with four replications, measured lint yield, ETc, WUE, IWUE. Q2: Section 3.3 and Table 3, WUE and IWUE compared between plant feedback (sensor-based iCWSI) and manually scheduled plots at 75, 50, 25 percent levels; WUE similar between methods within levels in both years; IWUE greater in I25C than I75 plots in 2013. Q4: Section 3.2 and Appendix Figs A.1-A.2, neutron probe soil water profiles showing storage at 30-110 cm and no deep percolation under the extra sensor-triggered irrigation; Table 2 irrigation amounts; Section 2.5.2 iCWSI calculated from canopy temperature; Table A.2 boll number and weight; Section 3.3 yield-ETc linear relations. Q8: Section 3.3 and Conclusions, false positive irrigation triggers from soil background at low canopy cover caused over-irrigation in I25C plots; 2013 valve miswiring reduced analysis to 21 plots (3 reps); larger standard deviations in plant feedback plots; limitations of temporal frequency and cloudy days; further research needed for the 25 percent level. Q9: Table 3, means with standard deviations for WUE and IWUE by method x level (e.g. C50 WUE 0.28 +/- 0.02, M50 0.28 +/- 0.02 kg m-3) and Section 3.3 text.
rows.notes: The study does report WUE/IWUE under sensor-based scheduling, but its own finding is that WUE was similar (not increased) relative to manual neutron-probe scheduling; at the I25 level the sensor system applied far more water than intended, so the claim of well-regulated deficit irrigation increasing CWP is only partly supported. Q3 no: WUE derived from a single method (hand harvest yield and neutron-probe soil water balance), no independent second method. Q5 no: single site, soil and crop. Q6 no: one half-pivot field divided into plots. Q7 borderline: authors note adequate canopy cover/NDVI threshold and higher irrigation levels (I75, I50) as where the method worked, but this is framed as explanation and limitation rather than a stated requirement; rated no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, two-year replicated field experiment with sensor-based (iCWSI) VRI control versus manual scheduling, hand-harvested lint yield from 10 m2 per plot. Q2: Abstract, Section 3.3 and Table 3, lint yields similar between plant feedback and manual plots at I75 and I50 in both years; significantly greater for plant feedback at I25 (142 vs 92 g m-2 in 2012; 109 vs 76 g m-2 in 2013) though with much more irrigation; overall mean yield by method higher for iCWSI plots in both years. Q4: Section 2.5.2 iCWSI computed from canopy temperature; Appendix Figs A.1-A.2 soil water profiles; Table 2 irrigation amounts; Table A.2 bolls per plant and boll weight explaining yield differences; Section 3.3 yield versus ETc regressions (r2 0.95-0.96). Q8: Section 3.3 and Conclusions, false positive triggers at partial canopy cover led to excess irrigation at I25C; 2013 valve miswiring removed one replicate; greater yield variability in plant feedback plots; further work needed for deficit control at 25 percent. Q9: Table 3, lint yield means with standard deviations by method x level (e.g. C75 182.4 +/- 20.5, M75 181.1 +/- 6.14 g m-2 in 2012).
rows.notes: Study supports that sensor-based scheduling produced yields similar to or (at I25, because of more water) greater than manual scheduling; the higher I25 yield is attributed by the authors to twice the irrigation rather than better regulation, so 'increase in yield' is only partly supported. Q3 no: yield by one method. Q5 no: one site/soil/crop. Q6 no: plot-scale within one center pivot field. Q7 no: conditions (canopy cover, higher irrigation levels) are discussed as explanations/limitations, not stated requirements.

notes: Full text appears complete including appendix. Same study rated for two functions (WUE and yield) from the same experiment; both claims share the caveat that the study's headline result is equivalence with manual scheduling at I75/I50 rather than improvement.
